questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Personal connection to the destination (heritage / friends there/ etc.)

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I am in complete love with Taiwan, and have always dreamed of coming back since my first time visiting this country.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I definitely recommend Taichung and Tunghai University to those studying Chinese, as there are great opportunities to mingle with the locals and speak their tongue as not all have the best English proficienties, forcing you to make a bit more of an effort.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Most informations were straightforward, some I had to fish out of some of the professors. It was not too big of an issue.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Orientation day and Jamie, our hero, truly helped us out a lot.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: Very satisfied with my trip, although some informations such as when our last exams would be, what they would entail were given to us very last minute.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I definitely recommend coming to Tiachung beforehand, and stroll along the streets of the Donghai Night Market, as there are a lot of student studio appartment rentals, where you'll see their Line or phone numbers plastered on the walls. These appartments are relatively affordable but get sold out pretty quick in the beggining of each semester, thus the recommendation of coming early. We were very lucky as to find a studio each within 2 days of our arrival.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Much better than the on-campus dormatories, as from the friends we knew who did stay there, they were pretty humid, horrible beds, and not the best accomodations overall. It is by far recommended to find a studio in the night marked area (look at my previous comment for aid).

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Not the best housing experience, but 4 walls and a roof is a place to live. It was already furnished with a Taiwanese bed, warning those are very hard to sleep on (literally), a table and a chair. We also got a mini-fridge, a wardrope and a TV. Each studio had its own bathroom with shower, so not too bad overall, as it had all the essentials.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: We managed...

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Most was done from home, so it wasn't too bad.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Jamie, the GOAT. She will help you with all the questions and confusion in the beginning.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: This was a mandatory stay, so pre-packed for us. Both my classmate I came with and I chose to also take Taiwanese courses on top of our mandatory Chinese, this is by far recommended, as it gives you a better insight into the Taiwanese culture through the unfortunately dying language. Very cool experience. It is also not mandatory, so it is pretty chill.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Always check your emails!!!!!!

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was tough, but fun!

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I was put in a class which was a bit high for my level, but it challenged me greatly. I am overall very satisfied with my experience.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Very similar, although everything was in Chinese of course.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Chinese and Taiwanese classes

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Taiwanese!! Do it if you get the opportunity!! It's so interesting and really allows you to understand the diversity of the use of Chinese characters in different languages. Such a cultural insight. Warning, the teaching is also in Chinese, altough, out of all my teachers at Tunghai, she was by far the best at English, so if you don't understand something, don't be affraid to ask.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Not that unexpected from a Danish perspective, but remember they have deposits when paying the first rent just like in Denmark. That is something to be prepared for. Generally, the first month, always expect extra cost for anything from buying an extra blanket, to a kettle for the appartment.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Remember to register your student ID at the city hall, it will allow you to travel for free every 10 km in the Taichung county.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Altar or 18, there aren't that many good clubs, but girls get in free most places, and students generally get in free many places as well. And sometimes they offer a free drinks wristband for a certain amount of drinks or limitted time. Pretty nice.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: The university offered many fieldtrips throughout the semester, so look out for the invites in the Line group.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: There's a lot of delicious food places to explore, and some cool cafes where you can study. It's also nice to go to the shore and watch the sunset, or hike the nearby mountains. Most of our classes ended around 12, so moslty we would go study at the library or a nearby cafe, but sometimes I would go hike, or we would visit Rainbow Village after classes, or try a new food place a bit further away and explore a new part of town! Taichung is roughly the size of Copenhagen, although it may feel larger due to the double in population or the huge skyscrapers everywhere. It is a really fun city tho.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Travel around the country, there's so much to see. If your schedule allows it, take a prolonged weekend trip to an island, or on a hike in the mountains, or visit another city nearby! There's so much to do.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I mean there is some adjusting especially regarding the heat and humidity, but you get used to it after some bubble teas. There are a lot of cultural differences, but that is why you go there, so go there with an open mind and an open stomack ;)

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Download the TimeLeft app, that's how I met a large portion of my local friends. They were not all students, but I had so much fun with them. Also go out, join many events, that's how you meet people. Taiwanese are similar to Danes in the way that they open up more when they are drunk, when sober they are quite shy and reserved... Like Danes, they prefer an event or a circomstance bring you together, it makes it easier for them. But don't be affraid to approach them.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: I personally had a pretty easy time fitting in...

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: People a genuenly so nice, truly helpful, even when you don't need it. It is so heartwarming.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Read your emails, always. 
Be openminded, always.
Relax and enjoy your stay. Don't force yourself too much!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: not sure, but there probably is

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: My friends there

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The language barrier sometimes, but you get around it. It is so rewarding as your understanding is constantly challenged.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: I am vegetarian, to anyone wondering about that, it is very easy as many buddist eat vegan/vegetarian diet.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
